tapeLine: Both inflation prints are in and they disagreed with each other: core PPI came in cool, core CPI came in hot, and hike odds for Wednesday jumped from roughly 60% to 86–90% inside days. Over the weekend a Saudi pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz was shut after drone strikes, and Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s own CEOs called for AI development to slow down — two shocks that have nothing to do with each other or with the Fed, landing on the same tape in the same week. Blackout runs through Thursday, so no official can respond to any of it before Wednesday’s vote.
matters:
Both halves of the inflation test this brief has been tracking since 4 September are in, and they split. August producer prices matched headline expectations at +0.4% m/m and printed a touch hot on a year-over-year basis (+5.4% vs +5.3% expected), but core PPI actually came in cool — +0.2% m/m against a 0.3% forecast — with more than three-quarters of the headline rise attributable to energy, up 4.2% on the month as the Iran conflict pushed oil through the index. Consumer prices told the opposite story: headline CPI matched consensus at +0.4% m/m, 3.4% y/y, but core CPI beat its 0.2% Dow Jones consensus by a full tenth, printing +0.3% m/m, even as the year-over-year core rate eased to 2.4% — the lowest since March 2021.

That combination is exactly the read this brief has been arguing for: it is core, not headline, doing the work, and the market moved on it immediately. Odds of a 25bp hike at Wednesday’s meeting, priced at roughly 60% a week ago, are now sitting at 86–90% across CME FedWatch, Kalshi and Polymarket. The blackout that began 5 September runs through 17 September, so nobody on the committee has been able to react to either print, or to what happened over the weekend.

What happened over the weekend is a second, independent supply shock landing on top of the first. Saudi Arabia shut its East–West pipeline — the one route that lets its oil bypass the Strait of Hormuz entirely — after drone strikes hit it around 10–11 September. The kingdom has five to seven days of oil stored at its Red Sea port before as much as 4% of global supply is at risk; the US energy secretary said Monday the line should reopen “soon” but gave no date. Brent is trading near $107–108, up roughly 3% on the session, and the 10-year touched 5.00% intraday Monday — a level last seen in October 2023, and one that would take out the pre-financial-crisis high above 5.02% if it holds. Two hawkish inputs are compounding at once: a labour market and inflation trend firm enough to hike into, and an energy shock arriving in the same week as the decision.

A third story is running in parallel and, for now, has nothing to do with the Fed: over the weekend Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay arguing the industry must slow the pace of frontier AI capability gains, warning that unchecked, “swarms of rogue AI agents” could contest control of the internet within six months. OpenAI’s Sam Altman and xAI’s Elon Musk both said they agreed. The call followed the resignation of an Anthropic researcher who accused both labs of “gambling with our lives.” It is moving equities directly — chip and AI-linked names opened Monday down sharply — and it is a separate, non-macro reason the Nasdaq is underperforming into a week the Fed was already going to dominate.

Invalidation: initial jobless claims held at 206,000 for the week of 5 September, unchanged from the week before, with the four-week average also flat. There is still no sign of labour deterioration, and no fresh wage data since the 2.6% six-month annualised pace already below the 2.7% pre-pandemic average. Nothing this week has touched the case the doves still have — that this is an energy-and-tariff hike being delivered into a labour market that would not, on its own, need one.

calendar.event: FOMC rate decision + Summary of Economic Projections

alsoOnTape: No US data is scheduled today. The next print is Tuesday's Empire State manufacturing index, then the FOMC decision itself Wednesday at 14:00 ET with the quarterly Summary of Economic Projections. Blackout has been in force since 5 September and runs through 17 September, so today's session trades on Friday's CPI, the weekend's oil shock and the AI-slowdown story with no Fed voice able to comment on any of it.
overnight: US Friday close — S&P 500 +0.86% to 7,656.98, Dow +509.19 (+0.98%) to 52,573.29, Nasdaq +0.96% to 26,333.04. Stocks rallied as CPI, while hotter than the 0.2% core consensus, still came in close enough to headline expectations to calm the tape, and as Brent eased 2.8% to $104.61 after Iranian state media said Tehran would meet Gulf states in Oman to discuss the Strait of Hormuz.

The weekend — Saudi Arabia's East–West pipeline, the route that bypasses Hormuz, was shut after drone strikes hit it around 10–11 September. Saudi has five to seven days of stored Red Sea-port supply before as much as 4% of global oil output is at risk. The US energy secretary said Monday the line should reopen “soon,” with no repair timeline given, and Iran is still refusing to reopen Hormuz itself absent US concessions.

AI — Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay Saturday warning the industry must slow frontier-model capability gains, citing a risk that unchecked “swarms of rogue AI agents” could contest control of the internet within six months. OpenAI's Altman and xAI's Musk both said they agreed. Separately, Altman told Fortune on Saturday that OpenAI is ruling out a 2026 IPO given unresolved AI-safety work, while Anthropic is still targeting a public listing by year-end at a valuation reported as high as $2.3tn.

This morning — chip and AI-linked names led Monday's open lower: Nvidia down 2–3%, Intel −7%, AMD −6%, Broadcom −3%, Marvell −7% in the opening session. The S&P 500 opened at 7,611.44 (−0.59%) and the Nasdaq Composite at 26,018.50 (−1.19%). Brent added a further ~3% to around $107.65 on the pipeline shutdown, and the 10-year touched 5.00% intraday, its highest since October 2023.

Gold — fell to a one-month low heading into Friday's CPI print, then extended losses Monday, down roughly 1.5% intraday to about $4,285, even as the oil shock escalated. Rising real yields, not safe-haven demand, are setting the metal's direction into the FOMC.

deals.what: Copart agrees to acquire ACV Auctions for $1.9bn in cash
deals.number: Announced 10 Sep: $10.50 per ACV share in cash, roughly a 45% premium to ACV's 10 Aug unaffected price. Structured as a tender offer followed by a back-end merger, funded entirely from Copart's cash on hand. Expected to close by year-end 2026, with ACV run as an independent subsidiary.
deals.readthrough: A $1.9bn strategic deal funded off the balance sheet in the same week a 10-year at 5% is the headline rates story. Copart didn't need a lender any more than WaFd or Tata did three weeks ago — acquirers with cash are still buying, acquirers who need debt are still waiting.

deals.what: Blackstone's flagship private credit fund caps redemptions at 5% for a second straight quarter
deals.number: BCRED, the $77bn non-traded BDC, received repurchase requests for roughly 10% of shares outstanding in Q3 (about $4.3bn) and again fulfilled only half of that, capping at 5% — an identical outcome to the prior quarter. Reported 3 September.
deals.readthrough: Same fund, same cap, same shortfall, two quarters running. Last week's brief flagged that generalising from three early-Q3 reporters to a decaying redemption wave was premature next to the ten-largest-BDC data showing 13–14% of assets requested against 5% caps. BCRED's repeat gate is a direct data point for that wider read, not against it.

deals.what: Solar Industries agrees to acquire South Africa's Omnia Holdings for $1.36bn
deals.number: Announced today, 14 Sep: Solar SA Investments will acquire all outstanding Omnia shares at 134.5 rand each, all-cash, valuing the explosives and fertiliser group at roughly ₹12,951 crore ($1.355bn).
deals.readthrough: Another all-cash strategic deal on the day the 10-year tests 5%. The financing-avoidance pattern this brief has been tracking isn't confined to US or even developed-market acquirers — still no debt-financed sponsor buyout has priced since this brief started counting on 10 September.

macro: PPI (Aug, released 10 Sep) — headline +0.4% m/m as expected, +5.4% y/y (0.1pp hot). Core +0.2% m/m, a tenth below the 0.3% forecast. Energy rose 4.2% and accounted for more than three-quarters of the headline gain, with the Iran conflict cited as the driver.

CPI (Aug, released 11 Sep) — headline +0.4% m/m, 3.4% y/y, both matching consensus. Core beat its 0.2% Dow Jones forecast at +0.3% m/m; core y/y eased to 2.4%, the lowest since March 2021. The soft-producer / firm-consumer split is the exact 'inflation is in services' read this brief has been watching for.

Fed pricing — a 25bp hike Wednesday is now priced at 86–90% across CME FedWatch, Kalshi and Polymarket, up from roughly 60% a week ago. The blackout has run since 5 September and continues through 17 September; no official has spoken since, or can before the vote.

Rates — the 10-year touched 5.00% intraday Monday, its highest since October 2023; a close above 5.02% would be the highest since July 2007. The 2-year, more sensitive to Fed policy, is at 4.654%, also a multi-year high.

Oil / Hormuz — Saudi Arabia shut its East–West pipeline, the route that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz, after drone strikes hit it around 10–11 September. Saudi has five to seven days of stored Red Sea-port supply before as much as 4% of global oil output is at risk; the US energy secretary said Monday the line should reopen 'soon' with no date given. Brent is near $107–108, up roughly 3% on the day.

Labour — initial jobless claims held at 206,000 for the week of 5 September, unchanged from the week before, with the four-week average also flat at 206,000. No new wage data since the 2.6% six-month annualised pace already below the 2.7% pre-pandemic average — still no sign of the spiral a hike into strength would need to worry about.
flow: Chip and AI-linked names led Monday's open lower after Anthropic's Amodei, OpenAI's Altman and xAI's Musk all called for slower AI development over the weekend: Nvidia down 2–3%, Intel −7%, AMD −6%, Broadcom −3%, Marvell −7% in the opening session. The S&P 500 opened at 7,611.44 (−0.59%) and the Nasdaq Composite at 26,018.50 (−1.19%).

That's a standalone equity story, not a rates one — it's arriving in the same week as the FOMC but isn't being driven by it. A hawkish Fed and a chip selloff are both pulling growth multiples the same direction at once, for unrelated reasons.

Gold fell to a one-month low into Friday's CPI print and kept falling Monday — down roughly 1.5% intraday to about $4,285 — even as the oil shock escalated. Rising real yields, not the geopolitical risk, are setting gold's direction into the FOMC.

OpenAI ruled out a 2026 IPO Saturday, citing unresolved AI-safety work; Anthropic is still targeting a public listing by year-end at a valuation reported as high as $2.3tn. Same weekend, same safety warning, two different capital-markets responses.
Breadth, dealer gamma, put-call and skew are paid data and are not on this page. Nothing here is positioning analysis — it is sector observation from the tape.

regime.tag: hawkish lock-in, two shocks, no referee
regime.sizing: A hike is now priced at 86–90% and the blackout runs through Thursday, so nothing expressed today changes before Wednesday's 14:00 ET decision — which itself carries a second live variable in the pipeline outage, a shock with no fixed reopening date.

secondOrder: Three stories are running at once this week and only one of them is about the Fed. The inflation data resolved cleanly in the hawkish direction — core PPI cool, core CPI hot, exactly the 'services, not tariffs' split this brief flagged as the tell — and pricing moved from roughly a coin-flip to a near-lock in the days since. That would normally be the whole story. Instead it's landing alongside an independent oil shock (a pipeline outage with no fixed repair date, sitting on top of an already-elevated Brent) and an independent equity shock (the two AI labs that have driven most of this year's market cap telling investors, unprompted, to slow down). None of the three moved because of the others: the CPI surprise was 0.3% against a 0.2% consensus, Amodei's essay was about model capability curves, and Saudi's pipeline went offline because of drones, not diplomacy. What they share is the same tape and the same week. A 25bp hike arriving Wednesday into a 10-year already at 5% is a different move than the same hike would have been at 4.5% — every existing floating-rate obligation, LBO or otherwise, gets more expensive at the exact moment growth-stock multiples are already being marked down for a separate reason. The financing story this brief has tracked since early September is still unresolved on its own terms: Copart, Solar Industries and, three weeks running now, BCRED's own redemption cap all point the same way — cash is still funding deals, debt still isn't, and nothing forces that to change before Wednesday. The test is now two days out.

scorecard.text: The 10 September brief argued “the thing to watch is core, not headline” and set the read as: a soft core PPI plus a firm core CPI would mean the inflation is in services and the hike case strengthens. Core PPI printed +0.2% m/m (a tenth under its 0.3% forecast); core CPI printed +0.3% m/m (a tenth over its 0.2% Dow Jones forecast). That is exactly the split described, and hike odds moved from roughly 60% to 86–90% within days of it.

The same brief quoted CPI as “expected at +0.4% m/m … core +0.4% m/m.” The actual Dow Jones survey consensus for core CPI was +0.2% m/m, not +0.4% — a meaningfully lower bar than what was cited at the time. The framing's conclusion still held because the real print (+0.3%) beat the real consensus (+0.2%), but the number the brief itself was working from was wrong.

Set the test as whether a large sponsor-financed LBO prints before the FOMC. None has: the two strategic deals that landed since (Copart/ACV Auctions, Solar Industries/Omnia) were both all-cash off the acquirer's balance sheet, and Blackstone's BCRED capped redemptions at 5% for a second straight quarter on 3 September. The test now resolves with the same event it was measured against — Wednesday's decision is two days out.
